column2: When adjusting the front crossview mirrors, which tire contact points should the driver be able to see?
column5: Front and rear tires on the left
column6: Front and rear tires on the right
column7: The front crossviews should show where each front tire meets the ground. They also cover the area immediately ahead of the bumper.

column2: A child disappears from view outside at pickup. After securing the bus and taking the key, where should the driver check?
column4: Along the curb and down the aisle
column5: On the steps and between the seats
column6: At the rear seats and emergency door
column7: A child close to the body of the bus may be hidden even with the mirrors correctly adjusted. The driver must find the child before moving.

column2: A school bus has no Park position. How should the driver secure it at a boarding stop?
column5: Low gear with the parking brake
column7: When the transmission has no Park position, select Neutral and apply the parking brake. Holding the service brake alone leaves out a required part of the stop procedure.

column2: Wind blows from west to east during a bus fire. Which equally accessible, traffic-free assembly area should students use?
column7: Students should assemble on the side the wind comes from so smoke travels away from them. Here the wind comes from the west.

column2: A student helper leads evacuees to the assembly area. What should the driver do before joining them?
column3: Walk the aisle for anyone still aboard
column4: Set warning devices on the roadway
column6: Count the students at the assembly area
column7: The driver checks the entire bus for anyone who remains, then joins the group, accounts for the students and checks their condition.

column2: A 38-foot bus faces a queue beyond a rail crossing. What minimum clear space does the handbook recommend beyond the far rail?
column7: The general guide allows the bus length plus 15 feet beyond the tracks. A 38-foot bus needs 53 feet by that guide.

column2: A blue railroad emergency sign displays a phone number and an identification code. What does the code identify?
column5: One locomotive assigned to the route
column6: One stretch of track between stations
column7: The code is the US DOT National Crossing Inventory Number. Giving it to the railroad dispatcher identifies the precise crossing where help is needed.

column2: During a routine route, where may a driver put a student off for misconduct?
column3: School or the student's assigned stop
column4: School or the next scheduled stop
column5: School or the nearest staffed stop
column6: School or the closest stop to home
column7: A driver may use the school or that student's designated stop. If the trip cannot continue safely, secure the bus and request help under local procedures.

column2: A turnaround requires backing at a drop-off. When should the driver unload the students?
column7: When backing at a drop-off cannot be avoided, keep students aboard until the maneuver is complete. Backing while students are outside exposes them to the rear blind area.

column2: During a pre-trip check, which movement shows a fitted crossing control arm has deployed as intended?
column7: The arm keeps a child's walking path far enough in front of the bus for the driver to see the child. The side-mounted stop arm serves a different purpose.

column2: What should a substitute driver adjust before setting the mirrors on an unfamiliar school bus?
column7: Set up the driving position first. Changing seat height or reach afterward changes the eye point from which the mirrors were aligned.

column2: A mechanic aims a substitute bus's mirrors for today's run. Whose eye position sets the sight lines?
column7: Correct aim depends on the eye position of the person who will drive. A mechanic can move the glass while that driver checks the view from the seat.

column2: A parked bus is surrounded by low cones during a mirror check. What is the instructor mapping?
column7: Targets at known positions let the driver verify actual coverage. No turning or other movement is needed for this check.

column2: Which defect explains a side mirror that repeatedly changes aim after the driver sets it?
column7: An unstable mount lets vibration change the mirror's angle. Surface damage can impair the image while the housing stays in place.

column2: A bus's window pillar hides a pedestrian at a corner. How can the seated driver uncover that view?
column3: Change the eye point by leaning
column4: Check the side mirror for rear traffic
column5: Look across the nose in the crossview
column7: Changing the position of the driver's eyes reveals what a pillar or mirror housing blocks along one sight line.

column2: Even with the school bus stationary, what creates a particular hazard for children along its left side?
column7: Traffic passing on the left can reach a child while the bus remains stopped. The normal entry and exit movements take place at the service door on the right.

column2: Which dimensions help explain why two buses can have different blind areas directly behind them?
column7: The length and width of the bus affect the rearward sight lines available in its outside mirrors. One bus's blind-area estimate need not fit another.

column2: Where can a small child disappear from view immediately beside a flat mirror housing?
column3: Low and ahead of the housing
column4: At the height of its outer edge
column7: The mirror assembly itself masks the area low and immediately forward of it. Seeing the side of the bus in the mirror does not resolve that obstruction.

column2: Which distant target checks the rearward reach of a school bus's flat side mirror?
column7: The handbook's flat-mirror adjustment calls for a sight line down the side extending roughly 200 feet behind the bus. The centerline directly behind it can remain hidden.

column2: A flat mirror shows the rear wheel rim but cuts off the pavement. What should its lower view include?
column7: The driver needs to see where the rear tire meets the pavement as well as the road extending behind the bus.

column2: A bus has stacked side mirrors. Which surface gives the wider view of adjacent traffic?
column7: The lower convex glass covers a wider angle. Drivers use it to monitor the space alongside the bus.

column2: What minimum width of roadway beside the bus should a side convex mirror show?
column7: The convex view should cover at least one lane on its side while retaining the bus as a reference.

column2: Which forward reference belongs in the convex mirror's view along the side of the bus?
column7: The side convex should show the flank forward to the mirror mounts. The ground ahead of the nose is mainly a crossview task.

column2: A car appears smaller in the convex mirror than in the flat one. What judgment could that distort?
column7: The curved surface distorts apparent size and distance. Finding a car in that view does not establish the size of a usable gap.

column2: Why retain flat glass alongside a wide-angle mirror on each side of a school bus?
column3: It shows objects at normal magnification
column4: It takes in the adjacent lane at a wider angle
column5: It fills in low ground beside the entrance
column6: It opens a view of the pavement under the nose
column7: The flat surface provides a view at normal magnification. The convex mirror expands angular coverage but changes apparent image size.

column2: At a stop, a lunchbox sits under the hood line just ahead of the bumper. Which view covers it?
column7: The front crossviews cover the low area that the nose hides from the seated driver. The inside mirror serves the passenger compartment.

column2: Where should the forward view in the crossview mirrors meet the driver's view through the windshield?
column3: Across an overlapping strip of pavement
column4: At the outer end of the crossing arm
column5: Along the line between the front tires
column6: At the first point past the mirror image
column7: Reflected and direct sight lines need to overlap. A strip visible in neither view could hide a child in front of the bus.

column2: Along each side of the bus, what should overlap the rearward edge of the crossview coverage?
column3: Field of the outside rearview system
column4: View through the side entrance glass
column5: View through the rear emergency door
column6: Field of the cabin rearview mirror
column7: Overlap between exterior rearview and crossover fields helps keep the near-side ground visible as it extends away from the front corners.

column2: Adjusting the right crossover brings the entrance into view. What should still be visible afterward?
column7: Correcting a blind patch at the entrance must preserve the front ground targets. Recheck both areas from the driving position.

column2: Ground targets sit at both ends and the midpoint of the front bumper. Which should appear in the crossviews?
column7: The joined fields should cover low ground across the whole nose, including the center between the front corner views.

column2: What visual reference belongs at the upper edge of the inside overhead mirror?
column7: Aligning the top of the rear window with the top of the mirror is a handbook reference for setting the interior view.

column2: An interior mirror shows the back row clearly. Which additional check tests its near-seat coverage?
column3: Heads of the pupils behind the driver
column4: Entire width of the rear window frame
column5: Exit step at the front of the bus
column6: Floor at the foot of the rear door
column7: The overhead view should include every seated pupil, even the students closest behind the operator.

column2: Which location inside the bus can the driver's own seat screen from the overhead mirror?
column5: Next to the rear wheel arch
column7: The seat creates a blind area directly behind it. Seeing a seated pupil's head does not guarantee a view low behind the seat.

column2: Which feature can give the driver a limited view of following traffic through the inside overhead mirror?
column3: Glass in the lower rear emergency door
column4: Glass in the forward roof hatch
column6: Low side glazing at the front entrance
column7: A glass panel low in the rear emergency door can offer a limited line of sight. The outside mirrors still carry the traffic-monitoring role.

column2: A car following your bus moves toward the blind area behind the rear bumper. How should you track its approach?
column3: Check the pair of outside rearviews
column4: Check the pair of front crossviews
column7: Outside mirrors let you follow traffic before it enters the central rear blind area. Losing its reflection does not establish where the car went.

column2: The crossviews show the area ahead of the bus is clear. Which views complete the exterior scan?
column7: A deliberate sequence covers the spaces ahead and beside the bus. Repeating one view can leave another area unchecked.

column2: A bus carries the federal caution label for crossview mirrors. Which task does that label assign them?
column7: The FMVSS 111 caution for the specified curved crossviews directs drivers to check for pedestrians while stationary. Those mirrors distort vehicle positions and should not be used to view traffic in motion.

column2: Which body reference belongs at the upper inside corner of a conventionally adjusted flat side mirror?
column7: The exercise uses the top rear corner of the body as an aiming reference. The driver should also retain the long view down that side.

column2: A pupil looks smaller in a crossover mirror than in flat glass. Which characteristic produces that difference?
column7: The curved glass changes the scale of the image while widening the field of view. The mounting position and aim determine which area appears in the mirror.

column2: A convex mirror shows the next lane but misses the rear tire. Which pavement should the driver bring into view?
column3: Front edge of the rear tire's footprint
column4: Back edge of the front tire's footprint
column5: Center of the front axle's shadow
column7: The side convex mirror should include the forward edge of the rear tire's contact with the ground as well as the adjacent lane.

column2: Which mirror should show a driver what pupils are doing in the rear seats?
column7: The interior mirror monitors the passenger compartment. The driver's outside mirrors serve the roadway and the areas around the bus.

column2: A family asks you to move tomorrow's pickup to its driveway. Who can authorize the change?
column7: The school district approves stops. Even a small move can change where children cross or what approaching drivers can see.

column2: What arrival margin does NHTSA recommend children plan for a scheduled school bus pickup?
column7: NHTSA's stated minimum is five minutes before the scheduled arrival. The margin reduces the risk of a child rushing into the loading zone.

column2: Which direction should pupils face while waiting at the designated boarding location?
column7: Facing the approaching bus lets the waiting group see its arrival and watch for the driver's signal to board.

column2: Students start toward your bus as its amber lights come on. What do these lamps tell other drivers?
column7: Alternating amber lamps warn that the bus is preparing to stop. They do not release students to approach or cross.

column2: A pickup bay lies to the right of the travel lane. Which signal announces the turn into it?
column7: The turn indicator tells traffic the bus is moving off the roadway. Pupil warning lamps communicate a different part of the stop.

column2: Why stop short of the waiting children instead of bringing the doorway directly alongside them?
column4: To see along the standing line
column5: To mark the place pupils cross
column6: To align the steps with the curb
column7: Leaving space makes the children move into the driver's view before boarding. Pulling alongside them can put them beside the bus before their movements are accounted for.

column2: At pickup, what follows the final check that traffic has stopped before students approach?
column7: Once the bus is secured, the red lamps and stop arm warn traffic. The driver verifies that the required traffic has stopped before fully opening the door and inviting students to approach.

column2: Why can opening the service door too soon bring a waiting group into danger?
column3: Pupils may take it as their boarding signal
column4: Motorists may take it as the merge signal
column5: Crossers may lose sight of the stop arm
column6: The waiting line may block the right mirror
column7: Young children can treat an open door as their invitation to move. Establish that traffic is stopped before signaling the group.

column2: Which count should a driver compare with the number that boards at a morning pickup?
column5: Riders listed on the school roll
column7: Comparing those seen outside with the number boarding helps identify anyone who was present but did not get on.

column2: Several pupils board but a regular rider is missing. What stop-specific information helps you ask about that pupil?
column7: Knowing which children belong at each stop lets the driver ask other riders about a missing person by name. An answer from a classmate does not replace checking for a child who was seen but is now unaccounted for.

column2: Students have started boarding in single file. Which instruction applies while each pupil is on the steps?
column4: Watch for the signal to approach
column5: Sit facing the front of the bus
column6: Wait where the driver can see you
column7: The rail gives support during the climb. Waiting for the driver's signal comes earlier, and students take their seats after clearing the steps.

column2: Which light should the driver switch on inside the bus for a pickup before dawn?
column7: The dome light provides illumination for boarding in darkness. External warning devices signal to other road users.

column2: The last pupil has just reached the top of the steps. Which instruction applies before the bus moves?
column3: Take a seat and face forward
column4: Wait for a signal before crossing
column5: Move beyond the end of the arm
column6: Stand where the driver can see you
column7: The handbooks direct drivers to wait until riders have taken their seats and face forward before starting from a stop.

column2: Just before leaving a morning pickup, the driver scans the path behind the bus. Who might enter from there?
column3: A late pupil trying to catch the bus
column4: A pupil crossing ahead of the bumper
column5: A pupil stepping through the service door
column6: A pupil waiting beyond the crossing arm
column7: The boarding count covers those originally present. A late child running up from the rear may be outside that group and already approaching the vehicle.

column2: The bus has stopped at a pupil's corner. Which of the driver's instructions releases the pupil from their seat?
column6: The request to prepare for arrival
column7: The bus must be stopped and the driver must release the pupils. The lights, door and arm are equipment signals and do not by themselves dismiss a seated rider.

column2: Six pupils are assigned a stop. Five step off, four reach the sidewalk, and three wave. How many in total must be accounted for outside before departure?
column7: The outside check must account for the five children who actually left the bus. Seeing four on the sidewalk leaves one child's location unconfirmed.

column2: A child's phone falls near the bus. Once clear of the vehicle, whom should the child tell immediately?
column7: NHTSA instructs the child to tell the bus driver right away. A child returning to retrieve something can disappear from the driver's view.

column2: A pupil's long backpack strap trails across the steps. Which point needs particular attention as the child exits?
column3: The stair rail and the service door
column4: The front bench and seat backs
column5: The lift gate and its platform
column6: The exit hatch and rear latch
column7: Loose straps and clothing can snag at the handrail or door. Observe the pupil until both child and possessions are clear.

column2: After passing a pupil's drop-off, which maneuver is specifically ruled out even if the roadway looks clear?
column7: Do not back up to recover a missed stop. Use the locally approved procedure, which may provide a forward route or require contacting dispatch.

column2: Which route gives a child a visible crossing position after stepping off a school bus?
column3: Along the roadside to a point ahead of the bus
column4: Straight across from the service steps
column5: Along the sidewalk to the rear corner
column6: Between the curb and the front wheel
column7: Walking forward along the sidewalk or roadside keeps the child out of traffic until reaching a visible crossing point ahead of the bus.

column2: What helps a child at the curb confirm the bus driver can see them before crossing?
column5: A view of the extended arm
column7: Eye contact establishes mutual visibility. The student still needs to watch traffic and follow the applicable crossing procedure.

column2: What minimum distance ahead of a stopped school bus does NHTSA recommend for a child's crossing point?
column7: NHTSA recommends walking along the sidewalk or roadside to a point at least ten feet in front before crossing. The child should also make eye contact with the driver.

column2: Before stepping down at a stop with a wide shoulder, where should a pupil look for passing vehicles?
column4: Along the left row of windows
column7: A motorist can pass illegally between the bus and the curb. Looking down the entry side helps a child detect that movement before setting foot outside.

column2: Where should a pupil walk in relation to an extended crossing arm?
column5: Between the bumper and the arm
column7: Going around the tip of the forward arm keeps the pupil where the driver can see the crossing. Cutting through the space behind it defeats its purpose.

column2: A pupil is about to step beyond the driver's side of the bus. What new hazard becomes visible there?
column3: Traffic masked by the bus body
column4: Traffic screened by the curbside shelter
column6: Traffic hidden by the right fender
column7: The bus can block the child's view of traffic. Before entering the exposed lane, the pupil needs to look again in both directions and follow the crossing procedure.

column2: A pupil waits at the road edge when an overtaking car sweeps past. Which message should the driver give?
column5: Give the signal to approach the steps
column6: Give the signal to join the waiting group
column7: Use the danger warning taught for that crossing so the child stays out of the passing vehicle's path. The normal crossing signal has the opposite meaning.

column2: Which detail best distinguishes a passing car from similar cars in a stop-arm violation report?
column7: A plate number can identify the individual vehicle. Follow the local reporting procedure and give only information actually observed.

column2: Why ask a pupil to remove headphones before crossing at the bus stop?
column3: To hear traffic and the driver's warnings
column4: To keep straps away from the handrail
column5: To free a hand for boarding
column6: To recognize the driver's hand signal
column7: Headphones can mask a vehicle or a driver's warning call even when the child is looking at the roadway.

column2: After unloading, one group crosses the road and another stays on the home side. Where should the second group go?
column3: To the agreed place away from the bus
column4: To the point for the crossing signal
column5: To the curb ahead of the crossing arm
column6: To the edge facing the opposite lane
column7: Prearrange where noncrossing pupils should walk or wait, clear of the bus. That keeps them distinct from pupils waiting to cross.

column2: What should the driver verify about a new pupil before the afternoon bus leaves school?
column7: A first-time afternoon rider may not know the authorized stop. Resolve uncertainty with the appropriate school official before leaving.

column2: Three older pupils sit on a bench rated for three small children. What determines whether they fit?
column3: Everyone fits within the bench edges
column4: Each pupil's feet reach the floor
column5: There is a handhold within each pupil's reach
column6: All their bags fit below the seat
column7: NHTSA recommends that every passenger fit entirely within the seat. Rated capacity assumes small pupils and does not establish that three larger students will fit.

column2: What is the reason for reducing most of the bus's speed well short of an icy pickup point?
column3: Limit the risk of sliding toward pupils
column4: Keep the boarding line within the door view
column5: Identify the children assigned to that stop
column6: Indicate a move toward the right shoulder
column7: PennDOT advises slowing well ahead of a slippery stop and easing into position. This leaves room to control the bus before it reaches the waiting pupils.

column2: Thirty children will now use a stop previously assigned to twelve. Which site measurement bears directly on that change?
column3: Usable space in the waiting area
column4: Length of the pupils' roadway crossing
column5: Distance from the farthest rider's home
column6: Sight distance from the curb to traffic
column7: The standing area must accommodate the assigned group while it waits clear of the bus and traffic. More pupils increase the space needed even if the street itself is unchanged.

column2: Children step off the sidewalk to see if their ride is near. From the waiting spot, which view needs checking?
column4: Across to the far end of the crosswalk
column7: The approaching bus should be visible from where children wait so they can stay on the sidewalk. Clear sight along the departure path does not establish that they can see their bus coming.

column2: A school asks its buses to stand close together in single file for dismissal. What hazard does this address?
column7: This arrangement reduces gaps where children could walk between buses. Follow the campus loading plan for spacing and order.

column2: You are checking the advance distance for amber pupil lights on a route in a different state. Which reference governs?
column7: The operating state's law supplies the advance-use requirement. Equipment specifications describe the lamp system, and the federal training outline identifies subjects drivers learn.

column2: A substitute driver knows the warning-light rules for curbside stops. What should be checked before the first campus drop-off?
column3: Local rules for signals on school property
column4: District rules for changing a pupil's stop
column5: State specifications for amber lamp color
column6: District guidelines for student crossing signals
column7: The use of signals on a campus away from the traveled roadway can differ from their use in traffic. Check the procedure for the particular unloading location.

column2: At a school loading area you must leave the driver's compartment to assist a pupil. After shutting down, what goes with you?
column7: When leaving the driver's compartment to assist, secure the bus and remove the ignition key. A supervision task does not justify leaving the controls available.

column2: At an afternoon drop-off, what should the driver look for near the stop that differs from the morning boarding check?
column3: People gathering to meet arriving pupils
column5: Children lining up for the first pickup
column6: Pupils moving toward the bus to board
column7: At dismissal a parent or other person meeting a child can be in the bus's path. The morning boarding scan also looks for children trying to catch it.

column2: A pupil at the curb has made eye contact with the driver. What should come before the first step into traffic?
column3: Permission to cross from the driver
column6: Warning to return to the curb
column7: Where students cross on a driver's signal, eye contact confirms the driver can see them. They still wait for the prescribed crossing cue and watch traffic.

column2: While pupils cross, why can closing a door linked to the red warning lamps be dangerous?
column3: The warning to stopped traffic may end
column4: The advance amber phase may restart
column5: The signal to following traffic may delay
column6: The side stop arm may extend again
column7: On a door-linked system, closing the door can end the warning to traffic. Follow the bus's controls and keep pupils protected through the crossing.

column2: Where permitted, which camera system is designed to document motorists passing a bus during pupil unloading?
column7: A stop-arm enforcement camera can record the passing vehicle while the driver monitors the pupils. Districts must follow their jurisdiction's rules on use and reporting.

column2: The bus is ready to rejoin moving traffic from the right shoulder. What indicates the intended merge?
column7: Signal left to indicate movement into the traffic lane. The pupil warning devices communicate the boarding stop rather than the direction of the merge.

column2: A line of cars bunches beside the bus after unloading. What should the driver allow before merging?
column3: A gap as the queue disperses
column4: A signal from the curbside group
column7: The California handbook's departure guidance includes letting bunched traffic clear. Recheck the mirrors and enter the traffic flow when there is room.

column2: A designated pickup bay is off the travel lane. When should the driver first reduce approach speed?
column4: As the front wheels enter the bay
column7: Reduce speed while still on the roadway. The bus should already be under control as it enters the area where children are waiting.

column2: At campus drop-off, which pupil movement should the driver confirm after a child sets both feet on the ground?
column3: Walking away from the bus loading area
column6: Gathering at the front of the line
column7: The driver follows each pupil past the steps and out of the loading area. The earlier milestones show the child has left the vehicle but may still be close to it.

column2: Which feature makes a rail crossing active even when it has no gate?
column7: Active equipment responds to a train. A crossbuck or pavement marking is present whether a train is coming or not.

column2: Which sign is placed in advance of a public rail crossing rather than at the tracks?
column7: The round yellow sign gives advance notice. The crossbuck and track-count plaque identify the crossing itself.

column2: Which part of a school bus determines whether it has stopped behind a painted rail stop line?
column6: Forward edge of the entry steps
column7: The front of the bus must remain behind the line. The front bodywork extends beyond the axle.

column2: A small plate reading "3 TRACKS" hangs beneath a crossbuck. What does the number describe?
column3: Sets of rails crossing the road
column7: The plate counts the tracks at that crossing. It gives no information about the number of trains approaching.

column2: Which pavement marking gives a bus driver advance notice of a railroad crossing?
column3: An X with the letters RR
column7: The X and RR marking warns approaching traffic about the tracks. A stop line serves a different purpose.

column2: On a rail approach, which hazard does the driver check with the outside rearview mirrors?
column4: An obstructed view down the tracks
column5: A short queue beyond the tracks
column6: A high crown between the rails
column7: The mirrors show traffic approaching the back of the bus. A following driver may be unprepared for the bus to stop.

column2: During the approach to a rail crossing, when should a manual-bus driver test the brakes?
column7: Testing the brakes during the approach leaves room to respond to a problem before the tracks.

column2: At a required rail stop, which openings improve the driver's view and hearing?
column4: Service door and rear roof vent
column6: Rear roof vent and passenger windows
column7: Opening the entry door and the driver's window at the stop improves the driver's ability to see and hear approaching trains.

column2: A defroster masks outside sounds at a rail stop. What adjustment completes the driver's listening check?
column3: Silence the defroster during the check
column4: Dim the dash lights for the check
column7: Turn off noisy equipment and ask riders to be quiet while listening for trains. Adjusting displays or transmission controls does not quiet a running fan.

column2: Three tracks share one crossing with no safe room to stop between them. If all are clear, how many routine rail stops are needed?
column7: Stop before the first track, verify all tracks and the exit are clear, then cross the group. There is no safe stopping place between these tracks.

column2: A freight train blocks the view down a parallel track. What hazard might its last cars still hide?
column3: A train on the adjacent track
column4: A bus waiting on the near approach
column5: A stop line before the first rail
column6: A queue behind the school bus
column7: One train can screen another from the driver's view. Wait for a clear view of every track in both directions.

column2: After the bus stops, the rail gate rises and the bell falls silent. Which indication keeps the bus stopped?
column7: A raised gate does not cancel flashing red crossing lights. Wait until the warnings clear and the tracks are safe.

column2: An exit gate drops across the bus's path after the bus has entered the tracks. The road ahead is clear. What now?
column4: Back up to the entry gate
column6: Wait for the gate to rise
column7: Clear the tracks even if the exit gate breaks. This applies to a bus already crossing, not one waiting to enter.

column2: A gate remains down after a train passes. No officer is directing traffic. Whom does the CDL handbook tell the driver to ask for instructions?
column7: Remain behind the gate and report the suspected malfunction to the bus dispatcher. A train passing does not authorize going around a lowered gate.

column2: What condition beyond a rail crossing explains a roadway pre-signal before the tracks?
column3: Short storage space at a signalized junction
column4: An oblique angle between the road and rails
column5: Low ground clearance over a sharply raised track
column6: Limited sight distance around a railroad curve
column7: A pre-signal can hold traffic before the tracks when a vehicle waiting at the nearby traffic light could otherwise span the crossing.

column2: A school bus approaches tracks in a posted quiet zone. What should the driver expect?
column3: Routine train horns may be absent
column7: A quiet zone changes routine locomotive horn use. A train may approach silently, although its engineer can still sound the horn in an emergency.

column2: Why can a bus be struck even after its rear bumper clears the last rail?
column6: Warning lights project onto the road
column7: Railcars overhang the rails on either side. The entire bus needs space beyond the train's actual path.

column2: A low-floor bus approaches a crossing marked for low ground clearance. What part is at risk as the front wheels descend?
column5: Outside face of the rear tire
column6: Front edge of the side mirror
column7: The underside can ground on a raised crossing while the axles are on opposite slopes.

column2: The bus stalls astride the rails. Which step comes first in the track emergency procedure?
column4: Notify the railroad of the obstruction
column6: Account for the group at the assembly point
column7: Get everyone off the bus and away from the tracks immediately. Start the evacuation without waiting to see or hear a train.

column2: A train is coming from the north toward a bus stranded on the tracks. Which escape route leads students away from impact debris?
column3: Diagonally north, away from the rails
column4: Diagonally south, away from the rails
column5: North, parallel to the track bed
column6: South, parallel to the track bed
column7: Move away from the tracks and angle toward the oncoming train. Debris from an impact can be carried ahead in the train's direction of travel.

column2: When feasible, how far should a proposed student waiting area be from an active rail crossing under NHTSA's planning guidance?
column7: NHTSA recommends maximizing separation and allowing at least 300 feet where possible. This is a route-planning recommendation.

column2: Which crossing hazard should a regular driver record as a fixed feature for substitutes?
column3: A hillside blocking the westward view
column4: A delivery van paused beside the tracks
column5: A fallen branch from last night's storm
column6: A bank of fog over the approach road
column7: A fixed obstruction affects sight distance on future trips. Document it as a route hazard and share it with substitute drivers.

column2: Which defect reduces a driver's advance notice before reaching otherwise working crossing lights and gates?
column3: Approach warning sign hidden by brush
column4: Damaged track-count plaque on the crossbuck
column6: Faded contact number on the blue sign
column7: Approach signs and markings alert motorists in time to prepare. Report a hidden warning sign to the appropriate highway authority.

column2: What does a skewed-crossing warning sign tell a driver about the road ahead?
column3: It meets the rails at an oblique angle
column4: It climbs sharply over raised rails
column5: It splits just beyond parallel tracks
column6: It has a short queue area past the rails
column7: This sign depicts a road and tracks meeting at an angle other than a right angle. A high-profile crossing and limited storage have different warnings.

column2: Where does a "storage space ahead" sign indicate room for a stopped vehicle?
column3: Between tracks and the next intersection
column4: Between the approach sign and first rail
column5: Between two parallel sets of tracks
column6: Between the entrance gate and its stop line
column7: The sign warns about the space available after the tracks and before the intersecting road. A long bus may have too little room there.

column2: A line of cars is stopped past the tracks. What limits how far the bus can pull forward after crossing?
column3: Rear of the nearest waiting car
column4: Front of the first car at the light
column6: Far edge of the intersecting roadway
column7: Only the open space up to the back of the queue is available. The bus must fit clear of the tracks before entering.

column2: NHTSA assesses track visibility from a bus stopped 15 feet from the nearest rail. What sight distance does it recommend in each direction?
column7: NHTSA's route guidance recommends a view 1,000 feet along the track in both directions. At multiple tracks the driver should be able to see them all.

column2: After a breakdown at a crossing, everyone is clear. Which number reaches the railroad to warn trains?
column3: Emergency phone on the ENS sign
column7: The blue-and-white ENS sign supplies a railroad emergency contact. A caller can report the obstruction and its precise location.

column2: An approaching locomotive looks distant and slow. Which judgment is particularly unreliable from the bus?
column7: Drivers cannot accurately judge the speed and distance of an approaching train by sight. Do not use a guessed arrival time to race across.

column2: At which stage of a rail crossing should the driver identify an escape path?
column4: During the listening check at the stop
column5: After checking the signals before moving
column6: As the bus reaches the first rail
column7: Plan for brake trouble or a threat from behind while approaching. Identifying a route before trouble develops preserves time to act.

column2: A minor crash leaves the bus secure off-road with no fire or other immediate hazard. Where should students wait while the driver assesses them?
column3: In their seats aboard the bus
column5: With a helper at the assembly point
column7: Keeping students aboard a secure bus helps the driver supervise and check them. Evacuate when the bus or its surroundings expose them to danger.

column2: Which crash scene calls for evacuation because the bus itself may move into greater danger?
column3: Bus balanced on a crumbling embankment
column4: Bus stranded across a blind highway curve
column5: Bus leaking fuel in a level parking lot
column6: Bus stopped beside an active rail crossing
column7: An unstable position can let the bus slide or roll into danger. The other situations present different hazards even if the vehicle remains still.

column2: Flames block the front of a school bus. Both end doors operate and the ground behind is clear. Which exit is preferable?
column5: Driver's side window at the front
column6: Roof opening above the front seats
column7: Choose a usable exit away from the fire with clear ground outside. For these conditions the rear door leads away from the flames.

column2: During extinguisher training, which motion releases the lock that prevents the handle from being squeezed?
column7: For the common portable extinguisher described in the handbook, pulling the safety pin frees the operating handle. The bracket and hose retainer hold different parts.

column2: Under the federal standard, opening a side emergency door past which angle to the bus body must engage its hold-open device?
column7: Once opened past perpendicular, the device must support the door and prevent it from swinging back through that position without another action by the driver.

column2: A crash victim reports neck pain. The bus is stable and safe. How should the driver handle that student?
column4: Help the student walk to the meeting point
column5: Seat the student beside the service door
column6: Have a helper move the student to a bench
column7: Suspected neck or spinal injury calls for avoiding unnecessary movement. Immediate danger to life can change that decision.

column2: On a school bus, how far from an emergency window release may its operating instructions be posted?
column7: The federal standard places the opening instructions on the inside surface within 15 centimeters of the release. The exit designation follows a separate placement rule.

column2: On an activity trip, who should already know how to secure the bus if the driver becomes incapacitated?
column5: The emergency contact at the school
column7: Brief a responsible person who will actually be on the bus. That person can secure it and summon help if the driver cannot act.

column2: For a planned drill, which task belongs to the student posted outside an exit?
column4: Guide pupils to the meeting point
column7: The exit helper assists pupils as they leave the vehicle. A separate leader takes the group to the meeting point.

column2: When helpers are available, how many older, responsible pupils per exit does the CDL handbook recommend assigning?
column7: The suggested arrangement has two students assisting at each exit. Another student can lead evacuees to the meeting place.

column2: Where does a school bus's reflective tape mark a required emergency exit for responders outside?
column3: Around the perimeter of the opening
column4: Along the side that carries the latch
column5: Across the upper and lower edges
column6: Across the panel at handle height
column7: Federal bus standards call for an exterior retroreflective outline around each required exit opening. It helps responders recognize the whole opening in low light.

column2: Following traffic runs east on a one-way street. The disabled bus faces east. Which equally distant, off-road assembly site follows the handbook's debris guidance?
column3: Open lawn west of the bus
column4: Open lawn east of the bus
column5: Courtyard due north of the bus
column6: Playing field due south of the bus
column7: The handbook recommends a safe off-road site toward approaching traffic. Traffic approaches this bus from the west, and a rear impact could send debris east.

column2: For a hazardous spill evacuation, what initial minimum upwind separation does the CDL handbook recommend from the bus?
column7: The handbook's initial spill guidance is at least 300 feet upwind. Conditions and emergency responders' instructions can require a greater distance.

column2: After a rollover both end doors are jammed, the left side is against a wall, and the roof hatch opens onto clear ground. Which exit is available?
column7: Choose the accessible, designated exit with a safe route outside. In this situation the roof opening is usable while the described doors and left window are obstructed.

column2: Both end exits and their paths are safe in a full bus. Which plan can reduce aisle congestion?
column3: Route each half to its nearer exit
column4: Send alternate rows to the rear
column5: Move both halves to the front
column7: Dividing the bus into front and rear sections lets both halves exit without crossing paths in the aisle.

column2: During a rear-door drill, how should an uninjured rider descend to the helpers?
column3: Sit on the edge and ease down
column7: The emergency doorway is high above the ground. Sitting at the edge and easing down lets the helpers assist the rider.

column2: A front-door drill alternates opposite seats. When should the driver release the next seat in this drill?
column3: Once the previous group clears the aisle
column4: Once the leader reaches the assembly point
column5: When the first pupil in that seat stands
column6: When the outside helper finishes a headcount
column7: In this drill, allow one seat's occupants room to leave the aisle before releasing those opposite. Other drill arrangements can organize rows differently.

column2: During a rear-door evacuation drill, how should students handle books and lunch bags?
column6: Place them by the unused door
column7: The drill practices a quick, orderly exit. Students retrieve their belongings after the exercise under the driver's direction.

column2: A belted student cannot release a jammed buckle during evacuation. Which tool serves this purpose?
column7: An emergency web cutter can free a student whose belt buckle will not release. Know its location before the trip.

column2: Dispatch already has the crash location. Which update best tells it how much medical help is needed?
column3: Number and condition of injured riders
column4: Number of students on the trip roster
column5: Number and type of vehicles involved
column6: Number of adults traveling with the group
column7: Give the number of injured people and what help they need. Total occupancy and vehicle details answer other dispatch questions.

column2: A resident relays a school bus crash report. Which pair of details identifies who is involved?
column3: Bus number and number of students
column6: Direction of travel and nearest milepost
column7: The vehicle identifier and number of students describe who is involved. The location and the kind of help needed answer separate parts of the emergency report.

column2: A working bus radio cannot be carried outside. Before evacuating, where can the driver leave its microphone accessible for later use?
column7: If circumstances permit, hang the microphone out of the driver's window so it can be reached from outside.

column2: At the assembly point, which record will help identify a missing student by name?
column7: Compare the group with the list of students actually riding. A capacity figure, stop list or list of contacts cannot identify a missing passenger.

column2: An investigator needs to reconstruct where each pupil sat at impact. Which record supplies that detail?
column7: The seating chart connects individual passengers with positions on the bus. A manifest records who rode; a stop list records where pupils boarded.

column2: Which information should the driver collect specifically from witnesses who saw a school bus crash?
column7: Witness identification and contact details allow investigators to follow up. Keep witness information separate from the student seating chart and vehicle details.

column2: After students are safe, what helps warn approaching motorists of a disabled bus beyond the flashers?
column7: Set out the appropriate portable warning devices to protect the scene. Their role is to warn traffic about the stopped vehicle.

column2: A driver's body-fluid kit contains several loose items. Which one collects used absorbent from the bus floor?
column7: The scoop and scraper pick up the used absorbent. The waste bag receives the collected material, and disinfectant is for treating the surface.

column2: A student asks when to leave the meeting place during an evacuation drill. Which event ends the wait?
column3: Release by the person supervising the group
column4: Arrival of the last rider at the meeting place
column5: The driver's final check of the rear seats
column6: Return of the exit helper to the group
column7: Riders wait at the designated place until released. Arrival of a helper or the driver's sweep does not itself dismiss them.

column2: A rear-door drill revealed confusion over a signal. When should the driver review what the group can improve?
column5: While releasing the first row of riders
column6: While the last pupils are descending
column7: Once the group is safe, evaluate how the drill went. Use the observed difficulty to explain and practice the step that caused confusion.

column2: Responders ask about the vehicles in a school bus crash. Which details from the bus's records belong in that part of the report?
column7: The vehicle section identifies the bus. Passenger information, scene conditions and witness contacts belong in other parts of the crash investigation.

column2: A driver buckles a preschooler into a five-point harness. Where should the chest clip sit?
column5: At the bottom of the rib cage
column7: The clip holds the shoulder straps in position. Place it at armpit height after snugging the harness.

column2: In a large school bus, which feature protects seated riders through compartmentalization?
column4: Raised aisle edges and padded armrests
column5: Low seat cushions and enclosed stepwells
column7: Closely spaced seats and energy-absorbing backs form a protective space around seated riders. This protection depends on the student's position within the seat.

column2: The bus is secured. Before stepping into the aisle to address students, what should the driver take?
column7: Taking the key keeps the vehicle under the driver's control while the driver's seat is empty.

column2: A driver assigns a new seat after repeated disruption. Which position matches the CDL handbook's recommendation?
column6: Row immediately ahead of the rear axle
column7: The handbook recommends moving the student close to the driver when a seat change is necessary. This makes it easier to supervise the rider.

column2: Which feedback reinforces a specific part of a rider's practiced bus routine?
column3: You kept your backpack off the steps today
column4: You look ready for a good ride today
column5: I appreciate having you on this route
column7: Name the action the rider performed successfully. Specific feedback makes it easier to repeat that action.

column2: Which repeated dispute over a bus seat shows the power imbalance characteristic of bullying?
column3: A group leader uses exclusion to intimidate a rider
column4: Two friends of equal standing exchange sharp insults
column5: Two peers take turns complaining about each other
column6: Equally influential classmates compete for the same row
column7: Bullying involves unwanted aggression and an imbalance of power. A rider can use social influence or the threat of exclusion to intimidate another.

column2: How does federal bullying guidance classify deliberately spreading a rumor to damage a bus rider's friendships?
column7: Rumors used to harm relationships are classified as social bullying. Saying something aloud does not make every such act verbal bullying.

column2: A rider reports missing possessions and repeated harassment. Which question helps identify an imbalance of peer power?
column3: Who could turn the group against you?
column4: When did the first incident happen?
column5: Where were the other riders sitting?
column6: How often did those riders approach?
column7: Social influence can create a power imbalance. Timing, location and frequency provide other useful facts about the incidents.

column2: After students are safe, which interview setup follows federal guidance on investigating bus bullying?
column4: A joint discussion away from classmates
column5: A witness panel with separate written votes
column6: Separate turns in a shared meeting
column7: Gather accounts one child at a time, away from other students. A private location alone is insufficient if the children involved hear each other's answers.

column2: A rider requests a sighted guide on a level, open walkway. Where does the rider walk?
column3: Half a step behind the guide
column4: Half a step ahead of the guide
column5: Shoulder to shoulder with the guide
column6: A full stride behind the guide
column7: In the usual sighted-guide stance, the rider holds the guide's arm and stays half a step behind to feel changes in movement. Narrow passages use a different position.

column2: A rider hands the bus aide a strip of symbols forming a request. Which aid is the rider using?
column7: With picture exchange, the student constructs and hands over a message using symbols. A social story uses pictures and words to explain a situation.

column2: A rider struggles to anticipate an unfamiliar sequence of bus stops. Which support explains what will happen through pictures and words?
column3: A social story about the trip
column5: A speech button for requesting help
column6: A card for requesting a preferred object
column7: A social story explains an event or routine through a short narrative with picture cues. A timer communicates duration, while a request card expresses a need.

column2: Which way should a student in an occupied wheelchair face during school bus travel?
column7: The securement station is designed for the wheelchair to travel facing forward. The direction the lift opens does not determine travel orientation.

column2: A four-point station is ready. How are the chair's securement points distributed?
column7: A four-point station secures the wheelchair at two front and two rear locations. The passenger uses a separate restraint.

column2: On a wheelchair without marked transit points, which component can take the straps if the manufacturer permits it?
column7: Attach a tiedown to a suitable structural part of the wheelchair as the manufacturer directs. Wheels and detachable accessories are unsuitable load paths.

column2: Which pairing gives crash protection to a student riding in a secured wheelchair on a school bus?
column7: The occupant needs upper- and lower-torso crash restraint. Positioning supports can help posture but do not replace the required occupant restraints.

column2: How should a removable rigid wheelchair tray travel on the school bus?
column4: Latch it over the rider's knees
column6: Fasten it to the lap belt
column7: A loose or attached rigid tray can injure the rider in a crash. Secure it separately before travel.

column2: Where should the lap portion of a wheelchair occupant restraint bear against the student?
column7: The lap belt should load the strong pelvic bones. A belt riding over the abdomen or chair hardware cannot provide the intended protection.

column2: A preschool restraint shares a bench with another student. Which placement does NHTSA recommend?
column5: Center the restraint on the bench
column6: Use the side nearest the buckle
column7: NHTSA recommends the window position on a shared bench. The other rider then has a direct path to the aisle.

column2: Which group does NHTSA recommend seating nearest the driver when laying out a school bus for mixed ages?
column5: Students getting off at the final stop
column7: NHTSA recommends starting designated preschool restraint positions toward the front so the driver can see and reach those children.

column2: Two child restraints fit individually on a bench. What measurement determines whether they fit side by side?
column7: The restraints and any other occupants must fit within the width of the bench. Each restraint must also be installed correctly.

column2: A driver checks a rear-facing child restraint on a preschool bus. Where should the shoulder straps enter the shell?
column3: At or just below the shoulders
column4: At or just above the shoulders
column5: Level with the tops of the ears
column7: Use the manufacturer-approved slots at or below shoulder level for rear-facing travel. Forward-facing harnesses generally route at or above the shoulders.

column2: Several riders laugh approvingly at repeated taunts without joining in. Which bystander role describes them?
column7: Reinforcers reward the behavior with a supportive audience. Assistants take part in the bullying, while onlookers stay passive.

column2: On an exposed school route, which part of a full-size bus gives a crosswind the greatest leverage?
column5: The roof over the rear seats
column7: The large side area catches a crosswind and can push the bus sideways. Strong gusts can affect balance as well as steering.

column2: A school bus travels through a tunnel during crosswinds. Where is a sudden lateral gust most likely?
column3: At the outlet into open ground
column6: Beneath the center of the roof
column7: The tunnel shields the bus until it reaches the exit. Be prepared for the side force to change as the bus emerges.

column2: Which light makes a school bus easier to see in fog without announcing a passenger stop?
column7: The roof strobe improves conspicuity. The other lights serve the student loading sequence. Follow local rules for strobe operation.

column2: A school bus must reverse. What is the lookout's job during the maneuver?
column7: The lookout alerts the driver to hazards. The driver controls the bus and chooses the steering path.

column2: Where does the CDL handbook prefer a lookout to stand when a school bus must reverse?
column7: A position inside at the rear window lets the lookout see hazards without standing in the bus's path.

column2: With ignition on, where must an unlatched school bus emergency door's warning be audible?
column3: At the driver's seat and near that door
column4: At the driver's seat and the first step
column5: Near that door and at the service door
column6: At the service door and outside the bus
column7: The federal standard requires a continuous warning at the driver's seating position and near the emergency door when its release is out of the closed position with ignition on.

column2: Which views should the driver keep checking while backing a school bus with a lookout?
column7: A lookout provides additional warnings. The driver continues checking all mirrors and rear windows while moving slowly.

column2: A bus turns left away from a straight curb. Which part may initially sweep toward that curb?
column7: The body behind the rear axle swings opposite the direction of the turn. A left turn can carry the right rear toward the curb.

column2: When should a driver watch the overhang while turning past a gatepost at school?
column5: Once the front clears the post
column7: The overhang moves as the bus turns. Checking only after the front clears the gate can miss contact at the rear.

column2: Where must the driver check the alternating red and amber student lights before a trip?
column5: At the front and service door
column6: At the rear and driver's window
column7: Both ends must display the warning sequence so drivers approaching from either direction can see it.

column2: The stop-arm indicator illuminates during pre-trip. What separate physical action must the driver confirm?
column3: Full travel of the stop arm
column7: A dashboard indicator does not prove the arm has reached its deployed position. Verify the actual arm movement and its lights.

column2: A seat cushion lifts free while its legs stay fixed. Which connection needs attention?
column7: The cushion must attach securely to the seating frame. Movement of the cushion by itself does not indicate loose floor mountings.

column2: Which lift control moves an empty platform from passenger-operating position into its travel position?
column7: Stow, sometimes labeled Fold, moves the platform into its storage position. Raise changes platform height during passenger operation.

column2: Where must the directions for backup operation be posted on a school bus's installed platform lift?
column7: The federal installation standard calls for operating and backup instructions permanently affixed next to the lift controls. The owner's manual can contain an additional copy.

column2: A school bus driver's checklist separates tread, handrail and lamp defects. Which finding belongs under tread?
column3: A lifting strip on the walking surface
column4: Movement at the upper rail bracket
column5: A crack in the step lamp lens
column7: The tread is the surface underfoot. Each option describes a defect worth reporting, but the others involve the handrail, lighting or stair structure.

column2: A school bus has a live passenger-camera monitor. From which position should its display be adjusted for viewing?
column5: Driver standing beside the entry steps
column7: A live monitoring system helps the driver observe students only if the display operates and is viewable when driving. A recording-only camera has different equipment.

column2: Which equipment pair does the school bus inspection identify for checking the condition of kit seals?
column3: First aid and body-fluid cleanup kits
column4: First aid kit and reflective triangles
column5: Body-fluid kit and spare fuse holder
column7: Where these kits are carried with tamper seals, inspect each for presence and an unbroken seal. A broken seal can signal missing supplies.

column2: An extended stop arm has paired lamps on each face. Where should those lamps appear?
column3: Top and bottom along the centerline
column4: Left and right along the centerline
column5: Upper left and lower right corners
column6: Both along the lower diagonal edges
column7: On a stop arm using the federal paired-lamp option, one lamp is at the top and the other at the bottom. Both lie on the vertical centerline.

column2: Which angle should a fully extended side stop arm make with the body of a school bus?
column7: The standard places the extended arm perpendicular to the bus side, within five degrees. The driver can observe whether the arm reaches that position.

column2: A school trip route includes an unfamiliar low underpass. Which bus dimension matters first?
column7: Compare the vehicle's full height with the available overhead clearance before choosing that route. A route suitable for a car may be unsuitable for the bus.

column2: A field trip departs at 2:15 p.m. Boarding takes 12 minutes. When must the bus leave parking six minutes from pickup?
column7: Plan backward from the group's departure. The bus must reach pickup at 2:03 and leave parking six minutes earlier, at 1:57.

column2: At what road width does NHTSA recommend avoiding a student walk-to-stop crossing?
column7: The toolkit recommends avoiding crossings of three or more lanes when a student walks to the stop or boards the bus. This is guidance for route assessment, not a state traffic statute.

column2: Which directions allow right-side pickups at Elm Street's north curb, then Oak Street's east curb?
column7: Traveling west places the north curb on the bus's right. Traveling north places the east curb on its right, so both stops allow children to board from the curb.

column2: NHTSA recommends considering advance warning signs near a curving school stop below what sight distance?
column7: The toolkit uses less than 500 feet near a curve or hill as a reason to consult the road authority about warning signs. This is a planning recommendation.

column2: A district maps a stop on the bus-door side. What crossing could its software still overlook?
column3: The child's walk from home to that corner
column4: The child's passage from curb to first step
column5: The driver's turn from the stop into traffic
column6: The bus's path from school to its next run
column7: A right-side stop avoids crossing in front of the arriving bus, but a child may already have had to cross the road to reach that corner.

column2: At an unavoidable turnaround, sight distance needs checking from which road-user perspective?
column4: Bus driver looking toward the pickup point
column6: Bus driver looking back from the final stop
column7: Approaching traffic needs to see the bus throughout the turnaround. Visibility from the student waiting area is a separate part of stop planning.

column2: Power fails on a school bus lift. What movement must its manual backup provide with a passenger aboard?
column3: Lower the platform to ground level
column4: Raise the platform to bus-floor level
column5: Fold the platform into travel position
column6: Move the platform to boarding height from storage
column7: The backup must be able to lower a loaded platform and raise an unloaded one. Follow the operating instructions posted at the lift.

column2: Vehicles turn into a shopping center at 10 mph. What minimum distance does NHTSA recommend between its entrance and a bus stop?
column7: For an entrance where vehicles turn in or out above 5 mph, the toolkit recommends placing the stop at least 100 feet away. Check applicable local rules.

column2: A driver brakes on an icy bend. Which loss of traction can functioning ABS directly address?
column6: Loss of contact over standing water
column7: ABS modulates brake pressure when a wheel would lock. It cannot correct a skid caused solely by excess cornering speed or power application.

column2: Which marking identifies a preschool restraint the manufacturer certifies to applicable federal motor vehicle standards?
column7: NHTSA directs providers to the manufacturer's certification attached to the restraint. The model number identifies the product but does not by itself certify compliance.
